_note: Invented example data for an AI email assistant. Not real company data.

workspace.product: Example: an AI email assistant inside Gmail and Outlook. It sorts the inbox, pre-drafts replies in the user's voice, and takes meeting notes. Sold to professionals on a 7-day free trial, then a monthly plan.
workspace.goal: Grow paid conversion in the US this half without hurting users' trust in drafts.

northStar.name: Drafts sent with light edits per active inbox per week
northStar.why: Revenue follows habit, and habit follows drafts people trust enough to send. Paid conversion is the lagging result.

drivers.name: Activation
drivers.definition: Share of new installs that send a first draft within 24 hours

drivers.name: Trust
drivers.definition: Share of drafts sent with light or no edits

drivers.name: Habit
drivers.definition: Days per week with at least one sent draft

signals.text: Drafts to first-time contacts get the greeting and sign-off rewritten about 38% of the time.
It writes to my clients like it writes to my team. Too casual for a first email.
Half of trial users never open the Drafts folder in their first two days.
Trial ended before I realised the drafts were already sitting there.
Scheduling emails are regenerated about twice as often as any other type.
I don't send drafts on emails with contracts attached. I can't tell what it read.
Switched away because the other tool books the meeting for me, this one just drafts a reply.
Love it, but I wish I could tell it to be more formal with certain people.
A built-in mail assistant shipped free tone presets this month.
A rival assistant now books meetings end to end from email.

metrics.note: New drafting model rolled out to all languages on Tuesday

memory.text: Goals approved. North star: Drafts sent with light edits per active inbox per week. Guardrails: Draft regret rate, 30-day paid retention, Cost per active inbox.
